title: How ast-grep Scans and Mutates Code
subtitle: Structural search and rewrite, from raw text to a fix an agent can trust
throughline: one statement, var x equals 1, from raw text to a parsed tree to a matched pattern to a rewritten let, and finally into an AI agent's hands

chapters.title: From Text to Tree
chapters.blurb: How ast-grep turns a source file into a tree-sitter syntax tree of typed SgNodes.

steps.title: From Text to Tree
steps.coverSubtitle: ast-grep is grep for syntax trees — so first it needs a tree
steps.spoken: Ordinary grep matches characters. Ast-grep matches structure, so before it can do anything, it has to turn your source code into a tree.
steps.displayNarration: ast-grep is **grep for the abstract syntax tree** — it matches code by structure, not text. Everything starts by parsing source into a tree.

steps.title: Pick the language
steps.spoken: It begins with a single statement, var x equals 1. Ast-grep first decides which language this file is, matching the file extension against the globs registered for each supported language.
steps.displayNarration: The input is one statement, `var x = 1`. **`SgLang`** resolves the language from the file's extension via registered globs — `SgLang::Builtin(SupportLang)` or a `Custom(DynamicLang)`.

steps.title: Hand it to tree-sitter
steps.spoken: With the language known, ast-grep loads that language's tree-sitter grammar. Tree-sitter is the parser that reads the raw text and builds the syntax tree.
steps.displayNarration: The chosen grammar is fed to **tree-sitter**. `lang.ast_grep(src)` wraps the source in a `StrDoc` and parses it with the language's `TSLanguage`.

steps.title: A tree you can walk
steps.spoken: Parsing produces the syntax tree root. From it you can reach every node in the file, the same tree the rest of ast-grep will search and rewrite.
steps.displayNarration: Parsing yields **`SgRoot`**. `SgRoot(src, language).root()` returns the top `SgNode` — the tree every later stage queries.

steps.title: Every node is typed
steps.spoken: Each node in the tree knows three things: its kind, the exact text it covers, and its range in the file. The kind, like identifier or variable declaration, is what makes structural matching possible.
steps.displayNarration: Every **`SgNode`** exposes `kind()`, `text()`, and `range()`. The `kind` — `variable_declaration`, `call_expression` — comes from the language's tree-sitter grammar.

steps.title: Concrete vs abstract
steps.spoken: There are really two views of the tree. The concrete syntax tree keeps every token, including punctuation; the abstract tree keeps only the meaningful, named nodes. You can dump either one to see exactly how your code parsed.
steps.displayNarration: ast-grep distinguishes the **concrete syntax tree (CST)** from the **abstract syntax tree (AST)** — `is_named()` separates real nodes from punctuation. Inspect either with `--debug-query=cst` or `=ast`.

steps.title: The parse pipeline
steps.spoken: So the journey starts here: source text, language detection, tree-sitter parsing, a syntax tree root, and a forest of typed nodes ready to be searched.
steps.displayNarration: End to end: `source` to **`SgLang`** to **tree-sitter** to **`SgRoot`** to **`SgNode`** — text becomes a typed, walkable tree.

chapters.title: Code as the Query
chapters.blurb: Patterns are written like ordinary code; metavariables turn them into structural wildcards.

steps.title: Code as the Query
steps.coverSubtitle: Write the pattern as if you were writing the code
steps.spoken: Here is the trick that makes ast-grep feel natural. You don't learn a query language. You write a pattern that looks exactly like the code you want to find.
steps.displayNarration: ast-grep patterns *are code*. You write `console.log($ARG)` and it matches any node with that structure — your old friend grep, but for the tree.

steps.title: A pattern is just code
steps.spoken: Say you want every console log call. You write console log with a wildcard inside. Ast-grep hands that text to the pattern builder, the same machinery that builds any matcher.
steps.displayNarration: The pattern text `console.log($ARG)` goes to **`PatternBuilder`**, which constructs a `matcher::Pattern`.

steps.title: Parse the pattern too
steps.spoken: Crucially, the pattern itself is parsed with the very same tree-sitter grammar as your code. So your query becomes a little syntax tree of its own.
steps.displayNarration: The builder parses the pattern with the target language's grammar, producing a **pattern tree** — the query is itself an AST.

steps.title: Tree against tree
steps.spoken: Now matching is just comparing one tree to another. Ast-grep walks your code's tree and checks where the pattern tree lines up, node kind by node kind. Every place it fits becomes a match.
steps.displayNarration: Matching compares the **pattern tree** to the **code AST** structurally. Each fit is a **`NodeMatch`** — `find` returns the first, `find_all` returns every one.

steps.title: Wildcards that capture
steps.spoken: The dollar sign parts are metavariables, the wildcards. A single one matches any one named node and captures it; a double one matches an unnamed token like an operator; a triple one matches any run of nodes, like a whole argument list.
steps.displayNarration: **Metavariables** are written with a dollar sign: `$ARG` captures one named node, `$$OP` an unnamed token, `$$$` zero or more nodes. The match remembers each capture.

steps.title: How strict to be
steps.spoken: You can also tune how literally to compare. Strictness ranges from matching every token, down to matching only the signature. And reusing the same wildcard name forces it to capture the same code in both spots.
steps.displayNarration: A pattern's **`strictness`** (`cst`, `smart`, `ast`, `relaxed`, `signature`) tunes how exact the comparison is. Repeating a name like `$A == $A` requires both captures to be identical.

steps.title: From query to match
steps.spoken: So a pattern is code, parsed into a tree, compared against your code's tree, with metavariables capturing the interesting parts. That captured match is what we rewrite next.
steps.displayNarration: Recap: `pattern` to **`PatternBuilder`** to **pattern tree** to **code AST** to **`NodeMatch`**, with **metavariables** binding the captures.

chapters.title: The Rule Engine
chapters.blurb: YAML rules compose atomic, relational, and composite conditions into precise structural queries.

steps.title: The Rule Engine
steps.coverSubtitle: When a single pattern isn't enough, you write a rule
steps.spoken: A single pattern is powerful, but real questions are messier. For those, ast-grep gives you rules: small declarative documents that combine conditions.
steps.displayNarration: Beyond one pattern, ast-grep has a **rule engine**. Rules are declarative YAML specs that combine conditions an `SgNode` must satisfy.

steps.title: YAML becomes a RuleConfig
steps.spoken: A rule is a little document with an id, a language, and a rule body. Ast-grep reads that YAML and compiles it into a rule config it can run against any tree.
steps.displayNarration: Each rule has `id`, `language`, and a `rule:` body. `from_yaml_string` compiles it into a **`RuleConfig`** in the `ast-grep-config` crate.

steps.title: Atomic rules
steps.spoken: The simplest building blocks are atomic rules. They test one node directly: does it match this pattern, is it this kind of node, does its text match this regular expression, or is it in this position.
steps.displayNarration: **Atomic rules** test a node's own properties: `pattern`, `kind`, `regex`, `nthChild`, `range`. `kind: call_expression` matches by tree-sitter node type.

steps.title: Relational rules
steps.spoken: Relational rules ask about a node's neighbors. Is it inside a class? Does it have an await somewhere beneath it? You usually tell it to stop by the end, so the search runs all the way down the subtree.
steps.displayNarration: **Relational rules** test surroundings: `inside`, `has`, `precedes`, `follows`. `stopBy: end` walks to the end of the direction; `field` targets a named child.

steps.title: Composite rules
steps.spoken: And composite rules glue everything together with logic. All means every sub-rule must hold, any means at least one, and not inverts a rule. A node matches only if it satisfies all the fields you wrote.
steps.displayNarration: **Composite rules** combine with logic: `all` (AND), `any` (OR), `not`, and `matches` for reusing a named utility rule. Fields within a rule imply AND.

steps.title: One verdict per node
steps.spoken: When ast-grep runs the rule, it asks each node whether it satisfies the whole thing. Every node that passes is collected, and the wildcards captured along the way come with it.
steps.displayNarration: The engine evaluates the combined rule against each `SgNode`; `find_all` collects every **matched node**, carrying its metavariable captures.

steps.title: Composed in practice
steps.spoken: Put together, you can ask something genuinely hard: find every async function that uses await but has no try-catch around it. That's an all of a kind, a has, and a not, in one rule.
steps.displayNarration: Real query: an `all` of `kind: function_declaration`, a `has: { pattern: await $EXPR, stopBy: end }`, and a `not` of a try-catch `has`.

steps.title: Rules, compiled and run
steps.spoken: So the rule engine takes YAML, compiles it to a rule config, and evaluates atomic, relational, and composite conditions against every node, collecting the ones that match.
steps.displayNarration: Recap: `rule YAML` to **`RuleConfig`** to **atomic**, **relational**, and **composite** checks, yielding the **matched node** set.

chapters.title: Scan and Rewrite
chapters.blurb: The scan command walks a whole project, matches every rule, and applies fixes as precise edits.

steps.title: Scan and Rewrite
steps.coverSubtitle: From one match to a whole codebase, fixed
steps.spoken: Searching one file is nice. The real power is running every rule across an entire project and rewriting what you find, safely.
steps.displayNarration: The **`scan`** command runs a project's rules over every file and can rewrite matches in place — search becomes a codemod.

steps.title: Walk the project
steps.spoken: Scan starts by walking the project directory in parallel, using the same ignore rules as git, so build folders and ignored files are skipped automatically.
steps.displayNarration: `scan` builds a **`WalkParallel`** from the `ignore` crate, respecting `.gitignore`. Only files whose language has a rule are parsed.

steps.title: One combined scan per file
steps.spoken: For each file, ast-grep gathers every rule that applies and runs them together in a single pass over that file's tree, grouping the matches by the rule that found them.
steps.displayNarration: Per file, `CombinedScan::new(rules)` runs all rules in one pass: `combined.scan(&grep, ...)` returns `matches` grouped by `RuleConfig`.

steps.title: A fix is a pattern too
steps.spoken: If a rule carries a fix, that fix is written just like a pattern, reusing the captured wildcards. Ast-grep builds a diff by substituting those captures into the replacement.
steps.displayNarration: When a rule has a `fix:` (e.g. `let $A = $B`), the **`Fixer`** plus `Diff::generate(m, matcher, fixer)` produces the replacement using the match's captures.

steps.title: Apply as precise edits
steps.spoken: Each diff becomes an edit, a start position, an end position, and the new text to splice in. Committing those edits rewrites our var x equals 1 into let x equals 1, touching nothing else.
steps.displayNarration: A diff is an **`Edit`** — `start_pos`, `end_pos`, `inserted_text`. `commit_edits` splices them in, turning `var x = 1` into `let x = 1`. `--update-all` writes the file.

steps.title: Report it any way you like
steps.spoken: When you're only reporting, the same matches flow to a printer instead. It can show a colored diff in your terminal, or emit machine formats like JSON, SARIF, or GitHub annotations.
steps.displayNarration: Without `--update-all`, matches go to a **`Printer`**: `ColoredPrinter` diffs, `JSONPrinter`, or `CloudPrinter` for SARIF and GitHub. Each match carries a `Severity`.

steps.title: Search to codemod
steps.spoken: That's the whole scan pipeline: walk the project, run every rule per file, turn a fix into edits, and rewrite in place, or report the findings without touching a thing.
steps.displayNarration: Recap: `scan` to **`WalkParallel`** to **`CombinedScan`** to **`Fixer`** to **`Edit`** to the **file** — or out to a **`Printer`**.

chapters.title: Built for Agents
chapters.blurb: The ast-grep agent skill gives an AI coding agent a deterministic, testable, structural way to search and rewrite code.

steps.title: Built for Agents
steps.coverSubtitle: Why structural search is a gift to an AI coding agent
steps.spoken: Now, why does any of this matter for an AI coding agent? Because an agent searching code with plain text guesses; ast-grep lets it ask about structure, and get a precise answer.
steps.displayNarration: The **ast-grep agent skill** ships as a Claude Code plugin. It gives an agent structure-aware search instead of fuzzy text matching.
sourceRefs: README.md: ast-grep Plugin Marketplace for AI Agents

steps.title: A skill, not a guess
steps.spoken: The skill is a markdown file that teaches the agent a disciplined workflow. Instead of grepping for text and hoping, the agent follows steps: understand the query, then build a structural rule.
steps.displayNarration: **`SKILL.md`** teaches a workflow: understand the query, then express it as an ast-grep rule. Text search can't say *find async functions without error handling* — structure can.

steps.title: Start from an example
steps.spoken: The first concrete step is clever: the agent writes a tiny snippet of code that represents exactly what it wants to find, and saves it to a temporary file. A worked example to aim at.
steps.displayNarration: Step two of the workflow: write a small **example snippet** that should match, saved to a temp file — a concrete target to test against.

steps.title: Write the rule
steps.spoken: Then it writes the rule, starting simple and adding conditions only as needed. The skill drills one habit hard: for relational rules, always stop by the end, so the search covers the whole subtree.
steps.displayNarration: The agent writes the rule, often via `--inline-rules`, starting with a `pattern`, then adding `kind` and relational checks. The skill's rule: always `stopBy: end`.
sourceRefs: ast-grep/skills/ast-grep/SKILL.md: Step 3, Always Use stopBy: end

steps.title: Test before you trust
steps.spoken: Crucially, the agent tests the rule against its example first, piping the snippet through scan on standard input. If nothing matches, it can dump the syntax tree to see exactly how the code parsed and fix the rule.
steps.displayNarration: The agent verifies the rule on the snippet: `echo ... | ast-grep scan --inline-rules ... --stdin`. Stuck? `--debug-query=cst` shows the real tree.

steps.title: Search, then act
steps.spoken: Only once the rule matches the example does the agent run it across the whole codebase, and ask for JSON output. Now it has precise matches with file paths and line numbers it can reason about or rewrite.
steps.displayNarration: Verified, the rule runs on the project with `--json`. The agent gets **structural matches** with exact paths and ranges — machine-readable, not scraped from text.
sourceRefs: README.md: JSON output for programmatic use

steps.title: Why agents love it
steps.spoken: This is the whole point. The search is structural, so it ignores formatting and noise. It's testable, so the agent proves the rule before trusting it. And it's deterministic, so the same rule gives the same matches every time.
steps.displayNarration: Three wins for an agent: **structural** (immune to whitespace and renames), **testable** (verified on an example first), and **deterministic** (same rule, same matches).

steps.title: The agent's loop
steps.spoken: So the agent's loop closes neatly: load the skill, write an example, write a rule, test it on standard input, then search the codebase and get structured results back. Structural search, all the way down.
steps.displayNarration: Recap: `agent` to **`SKILL.md`** to **example** to **rule** to **`ast-grep scan`** to **codebase**, and structured matches back to the agent.
